P.title: P.blurb
Human Body: How your heart, brain, gut, immune system and senses work.

P.title: bo-heart.q0.q
Human Body: Where does the right side of the heart pump blood?

P.title: bo-heart.q2.q
Human Body: Which vessels have valves to stop backflow?

P.title: bo-heart.q2.x
Human Body: Blood in veins is under low pressure.

P.title: bo-heart.c0.text
Human Body: The heart is two pumps side by side. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps it around the whole body.

P.title: bo-heart.c1.text
Human Body: Blood makes a figure of eight: body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body. One full lap takes under a minute at rest.

P.title: bo-heart.c2.text
Human Body: At around 70 beats per minute, the heart beats about 100,000 times a day and some 2.5–3 billion times in a lifetime.

P.title: bo-heart.c3.text
Human Body: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Veins bring it back, with valves to stop it flowing backwards. Tiny capillaries in between swap oxygen and waste with cells.

P.title: bo-heart.c4.text
Human Body: Blood is a little over half plasma (water, salts, proteins) and the rest mostly red blood cells, with white cells and platelets.

P.title: bo-heart.c5.text
Human Body: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red. They have no nucleus, live about 120 days, and you make about 2 million every second.

P.title: bo-heart.c6.text
Human Body: Blood pressure has two numbers: systolic (as the heart squeezes) and diastolic (as it relaxes). A typical healthy reading is around 120/80 mmHg.

P.title: bo-heart.c7.text
Human Body: Your blood type, A, B, AB or O, depends on markers on red cells; Rh positive or negative adds another. O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency.

P.title: bo-heart.c8.text
Human Body: Each beat starts in the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker, which sends an electrical pulse across the heart. An ECG records that electricity.

P.title: bo-heart.c9.text
Human Body: Press two fingers on the inside of your wrist below the thumb. Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Resting rates of 60–100 are typical for adults.

P.title: bo-brain.summary
Human Body: 86 billion neurons and how they talk.

P.title: bo-brain.q0.q
Human Body: How many neurons does the human brain have, roughly?

P.title: bo-brain.q1.q
Human Body: What part of the brain coordinates balance?

P.title: bo-brain.q2.q
Human Body: Do we use only 10% of our brain?

P.title: bo-brain.q2.o1
Human Body: No, we use virtually all of it

P.title: bo-brain.c0.text
Human Body: The brain has about 86 billion nerve cells. Each neuron receives signals through branches called dendrites and sends them along a long axon to other neurons.

P.title: bo-brain.c1.text
Human Body: Inside a neuron, signals travel as electrical pulses, up to about 120 m/s. Between neurons, at the synapse, they cross as chemicals called neurotransmitters.

P.title: bo-brain.c2.text
Human Body: The cerebrum handles thinking, senses and movement; the cerebellum coordinates balance; the brainstem runs breathing and heartbeat automatically.

P.title: bo-brain.c3.text
Human Body: The cerebrum's cortex has four lobes on each side, each with main jobs, though most tasks use many areas working together.

P.title: bo-brain.c4.text
Human Body: Each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. The idea of "left-brained logical" and "right-brained creative" people is a myth; both halves work together.

P.title: bo-brain.c4.viz.items.0.r
Human Body: Both halves work together in everyone

P.title: bo-brain.c5.text
Human Body: We don't use only 10% of our brain. Scans show activity all over the brain across a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems.

P.title: bo-brain.c5.viz.items.0.w
Human Body: We only use 10% of our brain

P.title: bo-brain.c5.viz.items.0.r
Human Body: We use virtually all of it

P.title: bo-brain.c6.text
Human Body: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's energy, mostly to keep neurons ready to fire.

P.title: bo-brain.c7.text
Human Body: Touch a hot pan and your hand pulls back before you feel pain. Reflexes travel through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain, saving precious milliseconds.

P.title: bo-brain.c8.text
Human Body: The brain rewires itself throughout life. Learning a skill strengthens connections between neurons that fire together; unused ones weaken.

P.title: bo-brain.c9.text
Human Body: Studies found that adults who learnt to juggle for three months showed growth in brain areas that track moving objects, which shrank back when they stopped.

P.title: bo-digest.summary
Human Body: From your plate to your cells.

P.title: bo-digest.q0.x
Human Body: Its villi give a huge surface.

P.title: bo-digest.q1.q
Human Body: Which nutrient has the most energy per gram?

P.title: bo-digest.c0.text
Human Body: Food travels through about 9 metres of digestive tract, from mouth to exit, over roughly one to three days.

P.title: bo-digest.c1.text
Human Body: Teeth grind food and saliva starts digesting starch. Chewing well means less work for the stomach.

P.title: bo-digest.c2.text
Human Body: The stomach churns food with strong acid (pH around 1.5–3.5) and enzymes that break down protein. Mucus protects its own lining from being digested.

P.title: bo-digest.c3.text
Human Body: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. Its lining is covered with tiny finger-like villi, giving a huge surface area.

P.title: bo-digest.c4.text
Human Body: The large intestine absorbs water and salt and is home to trillions of gut bacteria that help digest fibre and make some vitamins.

P.title: bo-digest.c5.text
Human Body: Your gut holds about as many bacterial cells as you have human cells. A varied diet with fibre feeds a varied microbiome.

P.title: bo-digest.c6.text
Human Body: Food gives energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Fat has more than twice the energy per gram.

P.title: bo-digest.c7.text
Human Body: The liver is the body's chemical factory: it processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen, makes bile to digest fat and breaks down toxins and alcohol.

P.title: bo-digest.c8.text
Human Body: After eating, stretch sensors and hormones signal fullness, but it takes about 20 minutes to register. Eating slowly helps you notice it in time.

P.title: bo-digest.c9.text
Human Body: Adults need roughly 1.5–2 litres of fluids a day from drinks, more in heat or exercise. About 20% of our water comes from food.

P.title: bo-immune.q1.q
Human Body: Do antibiotics work against viruses like the flu?

P.title: bo-immune.c0.text
Human Body: The body defends in layers: barriers keep germs out, the innate system attacks anything foreign quickly, and the adaptive system learns specific enemies.

P.title: bo-immune.c1.text
Human Body: Skin, mucus, tears, stomach acid and coughing all stop most germs before they get inside.

P.title: bo-immune.c2.text
Human Body: When germs get in, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and sore. Blood vessels widen to bring in defending cells: it's a sign the immune system is working.

P.title: bo-immune.c3.text
Human Body: Several kinds of white blood cells share the work: some swallow invaders, some make antibodies, and some destroy infected cells.

P.title: bo-immune.c4.text
Human Body: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock onto one specific invader, like a key in a lock, marking it for destruction.

P.title: bo-immune.c5.text
Human Body: After an infection, memory cells stay for years. If the same germ returns, the body responds faster and stronger, often before you feel ill.

P.title: bo-immune.c6.text
Human Body: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or version of a germ, so it builds memory without having the disease. Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796.

P.title: bo-immune.c7.text
Human Body: When enough people are immune, a germ can't spread easily, protecting those who can't be vaccinated, like newborns. Smallpox was eradicated worldwide in 1980.

P.title: bo-immune.c8.text
Human Body: Bacteria are living cells that antibiotics can kill. Viruses are much smaller and hijack our cells to copy themselves; antibiotics don't work on them.

P.title: bo-immune.c9.text
Human Body: A fever is the body turning up its thermostat. Higher temperature slows many germs and speeds up immune cells.

P.title: bo-senses.summary
Human Body: How you sense the world and hold yourself up.

P.title: bo-senses.q0.q
Human Body: How many bones does an adult have?

P.title: bo-senses.q1.q
Human Body: Why does food taste bland with a cold?

P.title: bo-senses.q1.x
Human Body: The nose does most of the work.

P.title: bo-senses.c0.text
Human Body: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, you sense balance, temperature, pain and the position of your limbs (proprioception), which lets you touch your nose with eyes closed.

P.title: bo-senses.c1.text
Human Body: Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus an upside-down image on the retina. The brain flips it and builds the picture we see.

P.title: bo-senses.c2.text
Human Body: The retina has rods for dim light and movement, and cones for colour. Three kinds of cones sense red, green and blue light.

P.title: bo-senses.c3.text
Human Body: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals.

P.title: bo-senses.c4.text
Human Body: The tongue detects five basic tastes; most "flavour" actually comes from smell. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose.

P.title: bo-senses.c5.text
Human Body: Adults have 206 bones; babies have about 300, which fuse as they grow. More than half of them are in the hands and feet.

P.title: bo-senses.c6.text
Human Body: Bones are living tissue that constantly rebuild. They store calcium, and the marrow inside makes blood cells. Exercise and weight-bearing make bones stronger.

P.title: bo-senses.c7.text
Human Body: There are about 600 muscles. Skeletal muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps.

P.title: bo-senses.c8.text
Human Body: Skeletal muscles move bones by choice; smooth muscle moves food and blood vessels automatically; cardiac muscle in the heart never tires.

P.title: bo-senses.c9.text
Human Body: The smallest bone is the stirrup in the ear, about 3 mm. The largest is the thigh bone, the femur, roughly a quarter of your height.

P.title: bo-lungs.summary
Human Body: How every breath keeps you alive.

P.title: bo-lungs.q0.q
Human Body: What triggers the urge to breathe?

P.title: bo-lungs.q2.q
Human Body: Roughly what percentage of air is oxygen?

P.title: bo-lungs.c0.text
Human Body: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, down the windpipe (trachea), into two bronchi, then branches again and again into tiny tubes ending in air sacs.

P.title: bo-lungs.c1.text
Human Body: The lungs hold about 480 million tiny air sacs called alveoli. Spread flat, their surface would cover roughly a badminton court.

P.title: bo-lungs.c2.text
Human Body: In the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out, simply by moving from where there's more to where there's less.

P.title: bo-lungs.c3.text
Human Body: Breathing is driven mainly by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs. It flattens to pull air in and relaxes to let it out.

P.title: bo-lungs.c4.text
Human Body: Your urge to breathe comes mostly from rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen. Sensors in the brainstem measure it in the blood.

P.title: bo-lungs.c5.text
Human Body: At rest, adults breathe about 12–20 times a minute, around 20,000 times a day. Each breath moves about half a litre of air.

P.title: bo-lungs.c6.text
Human Body: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. The air you breathe out still has about 16% oxygen, which is why rescue breaths work.

P.title: bo-lungs.c7.text
Human Body: Hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs. Tiny beating hairs called cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat, where you swallow it.

P.title: bo-lungs.c8.text
Human Body: Higher up, each breath carries less oxygen. Above about 2,500 m some people get altitude sickness. Over weeks, the body makes more red blood cells to adapt.

P.title: bo-lungs.c8.viz.unit
Human Body: oxygen per breath, % of sea level

P.title: bo-lungs.c9.text
Human Body: Breathing slowly, about six breaths a minute with longer exhales, activates the body's calming system and lowers heart rate within minutes.

P.title: bo-cells.q1.q
Human Body: How much DNA is in a single cell?

P.title: bo-cells.c0.text
Human Body: An adult body has about 30–37 trillion human cells of more than 200 types, from nerve cells a metre long to tiny red blood cells.

P.title: bo-cells.c0.viz.items.2.l
Human Body: bacteria living on and in you

P.title: bo-cells.c1.text
Human Body: A cell is like a factory: the nucleus holds the instructions, mitochondria make energy, ribosomes build proteins and the membrane controls what goes in and out.

P.title: bo-cells.c2.text
Human Body: Mitochondria turn food and oxygen into ATP, the cell's energy currency. They have their own DNA, inherited only from your mother.

P.title: bo-cells.c3.text
Human Body: Each cell holds about 2 metres of DNA, coiled into 46 chromosomes in a nucleus far smaller than a pinhead.

P.title: bo-cells.c4.text
Human Body: A gene is copied into messenger RNA, which travels to a ribosome. The ribosome reads it three letters at a time and builds a protein.

P.title: bo-cells.c5.text
Human Body: Cells copy themselves by mitosis: the DNA duplicates, the chromosomes separate and the cell splits into two identical cells.

P.title: bo-cells.c6.text
Human Body: Some cells are replaced constantly, others last a lifetime. Most of the neurons in your brain's cortex are as old as you are.

P.title: bo-cells.c7.text
Human Body: Stem cells can turn into many other cell types. They repair tissues and are used in treatments like bone-marrow transplants.

P.title: bo-cells.c8.text
Human Body: Cancer begins when mutations make a cell ignore the signals that control division. It multiplies out of control and may spread.

P.title: bo-cells.c9.text
Human Body: Robert Hooke named "cells" in 1665 after the little rooms he saw in cork. Van Leeuwenhoek first saw living bacteria and sperm cells in the 1670s.

P.title: bo-sleep.summary
Human Body: Why we spend a third of life asleep.

P.title: bo-sleep.q0.q
Human Body: How long is a typical sleep cycle?

P.title: bo-sleep.c0.text
Human Body: Most adults need 7–9 hours a night; teenagers need 8–10; young children even more. Few people truly thrive on less than 6.

P.title: bo-sleep.c1.text
Human Body: Sleep runs in cycles of about 90 minutes, moving from light sleep to deep sleep and then to REM sleep, when most vivid dreams happen. We go through 4–6 cycles a night.

P.title: bo-sleep.c2.text
Human Body: In deep sleep, the body repairs tissues, releases growth hormone and the brain's waste-clearing system washes away by-products of the day.

P.title: bo-sleep.c3.text
Human Body: During REM, the eyes dart around, the brain is very active and the body's muscles are temporarily paralysed so we don't act out our dreams.

P.title: bo-sleep.c4.text
Human Body: A master clock in the brain keeps a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm, reset each day mainly by morning light.

P.title: bo-sleep.c5.text
Human Body: As darkness falls, the brain releases melatonin, the "darkness hormone". Bright screens late at night can delay it.

P.title: bo-sleep.c6.text
Human Body: Caffeine blocks adenosine, the chemical that builds sleep pressure during the day. Its half-life is about 5 hours, so an afternoon coffee can still affect sleep at night.

P.title: bo-sleep.c6.viz.unit
Human Body: caffeine left, mg (from 100 mg at 3 pm)

P.title: bo-sleep.c7.text
Human Body: Too little sleep hurts attention, mood, memory and immunity. Being awake for 24 hours impairs driving about as much as being over the legal alcohol limit.

P.title: bo-sleep.c8.text
Human Body: People differ in their natural timing, called chronotype. Larks wake early easily; owls peak later. Teenagers shift later for biological reasons.

P.title: bo-sleep.c9.text
Human Body: Consistent times, morning daylight, a cool dark room, no caffeine after lunch and screens away an hour before bed help most people sleep better.

P.title: bo-skin.q1.q
Human Body: About how fast does hair grow?

P.title: bo-skin.q1.x
Human Body: Then it rests and falls out.

P.title: bo-skin.c0.text
Human Body: Skin is the body's largest organ: about 2 m² and several kilograms in an adult. It protects, senses, controls temperature and makes vitamin D.

P.title: bo-skin.c1.text
Human Body: The epidermis is the protective outer layer, the dermis holds nerves, blood vessels, sweat glands and hair roots, and the fatty layer beneath insulates and cushions.

P.title: bo-skin.c2.text
Human Body: You shed tens of thousands of dead skin cells every minute. The outer layer replaces itself roughly every month; much household dust contains skin flakes.

P.title: bo-skin.c2.viz.steps.0
Human Body: New cells form at the base

P.title: bo-skin.c3.text
Human Body: Sweat cools you as it evaporates. Humans have 2–4 million sweat glands, one reason we're among the best long-distance runners in the animal world.

P.title: bo-skin.c4.text
Human Body: Skin colour comes from melanin, which absorbs UV light. Human populations evolved different amounts depending on sunlight where their ancestors lived.

P.title: bo-skin.c5.text
Human Body: UV radiation damages skin DNA, causing sunburn, ageing and skin cancer. Shade, clothing and sunscreen with SPF 30 or more help, especially at midday.

P.title: bo-skin.c6.text
Human Body: You have about 5 million hair follicles, and around 100,000 on your scalp. Each hair grows about 1 cm a month, then rests and falls out.

P.title: bo-skin.c7.text
Human Body: Goosebumps are tiny muscles pulling hairs upright. In furry ancestors it trapped warm air or made them look bigger; in us it's mostly a leftover.

P.title: bo-skin.c8.text
Human Body: Nails are made of keratin, like hair. Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month, faster than toenails, and faster in summer.

P.title: bo-skin.c9.text
Human Body: A cut heals in stages: bleeding stops with a clot, white cells clean the wound, new tissue fills it and a scar slowly remodels over months.

P.title: bo-hormones.q1.q
Human Body: Why is table salt often iodised?

P.title: bo-hormones.c0.text
Human Body: Hormones are messengers released into the blood by glands. They travel everywhere but only act on cells with the right receptors, like a key fitting a lock.

P.title: bo-hormones.c1.text
Human Body: Nerves send fast, precise signals; hormones send slower, longer-lasting, widespread signals.

P.title: bo-hormones.c2.text
Human Body: Key glands include the pituitary (the "master gland"), thyroid, adrenals, pancreas and the ovaries or testes.

P.title: bo-hormones.c3.text
Human Body: After a meal, the pancreas releases insulin, which lets cells take up sugar from the blood. Glucagon does the opposite when sugar runs low.

P.title: bo-hormones.c4.text
Human Body: In a fright, the adrenal glands release adrenaline within seconds: faster heart, wider airways, more sugar in the blood. Ready to act.

P.title: bo-hormones.c5.text
Human Body: Cortisol is released during longer stress and follows a daily rhythm, peaking soon after waking. Chronically high levels can affect sleep and immunity.

P.title: bo-hormones.c6.text
Human Body: The thyroid in your neck sets your metabolic rate, how fast your body uses energy. It needs iodine, which is why table salt is often iodised.

P.title: bo-hormones.c7.text
Human Body: Growth hormone from the pituitary drives growth in childhood and is mostly released during deep sleep. It also helps repair tissues in adults.

P.title: bo-hormones.c8.text
Human Body: Ghrelin rises before meals and makes you hungry; leptin, from fat tissue, signals you have enough stored energy.

P.title: bo-hormones.c9.text
Human Body: Most hormones work like a thermostat: when a level rises too high, a signal shuts down production, keeping things balanced.

P.title: bo-kidneys.q0.q
Human Body: How much blood plasma do the kidneys filter daily?

P.title: bo-kidneys.q2.q
Human Body: Can people live with one kidney?

P.title: bo-kidneys.q2.o1
Human Body: Yes, one healthy kidney is enough

P.title: bo-kidneys.c0.text
Human Body: You have two fist-sized kidneys at the back of your abdomen. Together they filter about 180 litres of blood plasma a day and return almost all of it.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c1.text
Human Body: Each kidney contains about a million tiny filtering units called nephrons. They let water and small molecules through, then reabsorb what the body needs.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c2.text
Human Body: Kidneys remove urea (from protein breakdown), extra salt, excess water and many medicines, keeping blood chemistry within tight limits.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c3.text
Human Body: When you're short of water, the brain releases a hormone that makes kidneys save it, so urine gets darker. Drink plenty and urine is pale.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c4.text
Human Body: Pale straw colour usually means you're well hydrated; dark amber suggests you need to drink. Some foods and vitamins change colour too.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c5.text
Human Body: Kidneys help control blood pressure by adjusting how much salt and water the body keeps, and by releasing hormones that tighten blood vessels.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c6.text
Human Body: Kidneys also make a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells, and activate vitamin D for strong bones.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c7.text
Human Body: Minerals in urine can crystallise into stones, which can be very painful when they move. Drinking enough water is the main prevention.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c8.text
Human Body: One healthy kidney can do the work of two, which is why living kidney donation is possible. The first successful kidney transplant was in 1954.

P.title: bo-kidneys.c9.text
Human Body: The bladder stores urine, holding about 400–600 ml. Stretch sensors signal the urge to go well before it's full.

P.title: bo-muscles.summary
Human Body: How movement works and why it matters.

P.title: bo-muscles.q1.q
Human Body: How much moderate activity does the WHO recommend weekly?

P.title: bo-muscles.q1.x
Human Body: Plus strength training twice a week.

P.title: bo-muscles.c0.text
Human Body: Muscle fibres contain filaments that slide past each other, pulled by tiny molecular "oars". Billions of them shortening together make a muscle contract.

P.title: bo-muscles.c1.text
Human Body: Slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue and suit endurance; fast-twitch fibres are powerful but tire quickly. Marathon runners and sprinters have different mixes.

P.title: bo-muscles.c2.text
Human Body: For a few seconds, muscles use stored fuel; for about a minute, they burn sugar without oxygen, making lactate; beyond that, they rely on oxygen.

P.title: bo-muscles.c3.text
Human Body: Strength training creates small damage and stress in fibres. During recovery, the body rebuilds them thicker and stronger, if you eat enough protein and rest.

P.title: bo-muscles.c4.text
Human Body: Without use, muscles shrink quickly; a week in bed can cost noticeable strength. From around 30–40, muscle mass declines slowly unless you train.

P.title: bo-muscles.c5.text
Human Body: Aerobic exercise strengthens the heart, lowers blood pressure and resting heart rate, and improves mood and sleep.

P.title: bo-muscles.c6.text
Human Body: The WHO recommends adults get 150–300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening at least twice a week.

P.title: bo-muscles.c7.text
Human Body: A warm-up raises muscle temperature and readies joints. Dynamic movements before exercise work better than long static stretches.

P.title: bo-muscles.c8.text
Human Body: Muscle soreness a day or two after unusual exercise is normal and comes from small fibre damage, not "lactic acid build-up".

P.title: bo-muscles.c8.viz.items.0.r
Human Body: Small fibre damage and repair do

P.title: bo-muscles.c9.text
Human Body: Even short bursts help. Taking the stairs, walking during calls and a 10-minute walk after meals add up and improve blood sugar.

P.title: bo-life.summary
Human Body: From a single cell to old age.

P.title: bo-life.q0.q
Human Body: When does the brain's planning region finish maturing?

P.title: bo-life.q1.q
Human Body: How many bones does a newborn have?

P.title: bo-life.c0.text
Human Body: You began as a single fertilised egg. By birth, after about 40 weeks, you had trillions of cells organised into organs.

P.title: bo-life.c1.text
Human Body: Newborns have about 300 bones, can't see far and can recognise their mother's voice, heard in the womb.

P.title: bo-life.c2.text
Human Body: A baby's brain doubles in size in the first year. Billions of connections form; unused ones are later pruned.

P.title: bo-life.c3.text
Human Body: Hormones from the brain trigger puberty, usually between about 8 and 14. Growth spurts, voice changes and brain reorganisation follow.

P.title: bo-life.c4.text
Human Body: The prefrontal cortex, which handles planning and self-control, keeps maturing until the mid-20s, while reward systems mature earlier.

P.title: bo-life.c5.text
Human Body: Different abilities peak at different ages. Speed and muscle often peak in the 20s; vocabulary and knowledge keep growing into the 60s and beyond.

P.title: bo-life.c6.text
Human Body: Ageing comes from accumulated damage: DNA errors, worn proteins, shrinking chromosome tips called telomeres and cells that stop dividing.

P.title: bo-life.c7.text
Human Body: Life expectancy at birth in Portugal rose from about 63 in 1960 to over 81 today, thanks to vaccines, clean water, nutrition and healthcare.

P.title: bo-life.c8.text
Human Body: Regions where people often live past 100, like Okinawa and Sardinia, share habits: daily movement, plant-rich diets, strong social ties and purpose.

P.title: bo-life.c9.text
Human Body: Evidence points to a few big levers: stay active, keep muscles strong, sleep well, don't smoke, keep learning and stay connected with people.

P.title: bo-genes.summary
Human Body: Why you look like your family.

P.title: bo-genes.q0.q
Human Body: Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child because…

P.title: bo-genes.q0.o1
Human Body: both carry a recessive blue version

P.title: bo-genes.q0.x
Human Body: A 1 in 4 chance if both are Bb.

P.title: bo-genes.q1.q
Human Body: Who discovered the basic rules of inheritance?

P.title: bo-genes.c0.text
Human Body: You inherit 23 chromosomes from your mother and 23 from your father. Each pair carries two versions of most genes.

P.title: bo-genes.c1.text
Human Body: In the 1860s, monk Gregor Mendel bred pea plants and found traits pass in predictable ratios. He's the father of genetics, though ignored until 1900.

P.title: bo-genes.c2.text
Human Body: A dominant version shows up if you have one copy; a recessive one only shows if you have two. Two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

P.title: bo-genes.c3.text
Human Body: Usually, two X chromosomes lead to female development and an X with a Y to male. The father's sperm carries either an X or a Y.

P.title: bo-genes.c4.text
Human Body: Height, intelligence and most diseases are shaped by hundreds of genes plus environment. There's no single "height gene".

P.title: bo-genes.c5.text
Human Body: Twin studies compare identical and non-identical twins to estimate how much variation comes from genes. For most traits, both matter a lot.

P.title: bo-genes.c6.text
Human Body: Completed in 2003, it read the 3 billion letters of human DNA. The first genome cost about $3 billion; today one costs a few hundred dollars.

P.title: bo-genes.c7.text
Human Body: Any two people share about 99.9% of their DNA. Humans also share about 98–99% with chimpanzees and around 60% of genes with bananas.

P.title: bo-genes.c8.text
Human Body: Chemical tags on DNA switch genes on and off without changing the code. Diet, stress and environment can change these tags.

P.title: bo-genes.c9.text
Human Body: CRISPR, developed in 2012, lets scientists cut and edit DNA precisely. In 2023 the first CRISPR-based treatment was approved, for sickle cell disease.

P.title: bo-teeth.q0.q
Human Body: What is the hardest substance in the body?

P.title: bo-teeth.c0.text
Human Body: Children have 20 baby teeth; adults have up to 32 permanent ones, including four wisdom teeth that often appear late, or never.

P.title: bo-teeth.c1.text
Human Body: Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, covers the crown. Beneath is dentine, and in the centre the pulp with nerves and blood vessels.

P.title: bo-teeth.c2.text
Human Body: Bacteria in plaque eat sugars and make acid. Acid dissolves enamel; repeated attacks create a hole, a cavity.

P.title: bo-teeth.c3.text
Human Body: Each sugary snack starts a 20–30 minute acid attack. Sipping sweet drinks all day is worse for teeth than having the same sugar at once.

P.title: bo-teeth.c4.text
Human Body: Fluoride makes enamel more resistant to acid and helps repair early damage. Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste is the main protection.

P.title: bo-teeth.c5.text
Human Body: Brush for two minutes, twice a day, then spit but don't rinse, so fluoride stays on teeth. Floss or interdental brushes clean between teeth.

P.title: bo-teeth.c6.text
Human Body: Gum disease starts with bleeding gums and can lead to tooth loss. It's linked to heart disease and diabetes too.

P.title: bo-teeth.c7.text
Human Body: You make about 0.5–1.5 litres of saliva a day. It washes teeth, neutralises acid, starts digestion and helps you taste.

P.title: bo-teeth.c8.text
Human Body: Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars crush. Our mix of teeth reflects an omnivore's diet.

P.title: bo-teeth.c9.text
Human Body: Teeth record your life: archaeologists read diet, age and even where someone grew up from chemicals in tooth enamel.

P.title: bo-medicine.q0.q
Human Body: Who showed that handwashing saves lives?

P.title: bo-medicine.q2.x
Human Body: The heart pumps blood around the body.

P.title: bo-medicine.c0.text
Human Body: Around 400 BCE, Hippocrates taught that diseases have natural causes, not divine ones, and that doctors should observe carefully. The Hippocratic Oath is named after him.

P.title: bo-medicine.c1.text
Human Body: For 2,000 years, doctors believed health depended on balancing four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. It led to bloodletting, which often did harm.

P.title: bo-medicine.c2.text
Human Body: In 1543 Andreas Vesalius published accurate drawings of the human body from dissections, correcting many errors that had been believed since ancient times.

P.title: bo-medicine.c3.text
Human Body: In 1628 William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood around the body in a closed loop, rather than the liver constantly making new blood.

P.title: bo-medicine.c4.text
Human Body: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that microbes cause many diseases. It transformed medicine, food safety and hygiene.

P.title: bo-medicine.c5.text
Human Body: In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths of new mothers dramatically by making doctors wash their hands. Colleagues mocked him; he was proved right after his death.

P.title: bo-medicine.c6.text
Human Body: Surgery before 1846 meant enduring pain fully awake. Ether, and then chloroform, made long, careful operations possible.

P.title: bo-medicine.c7.text
Human Body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a plate. Developed into a drug in the 1940s, penicillin and later antibiotics saved hundreds of millions of lives.

P.title: bo-medicine.c8.text
Human Body: Egas Moniz won Portugal's first Nobel Prize, in 1949, for the lobotomy, now abandoned and controversial. His invention of cerebral angiography, imaging brain blood vessels, has lasted.

P.title: bo-medicine.c9.text
Human Body: Recent decades brought imaging scans, organ transplants, keyhole surgery, mRNA vaccines and targeted cancer drugs.

P.title: bo-nutrition.q0.q
Human Body: Which vitamin did sailors lack when they got scurvy?

P.title: bo-nutrition.q1.q
Human Body: What reduces iron absorption from a meal?

P.title: bo-nutrition.c0.text
Human Body: Vitamins are compounds the body needs in tiny amounts but mostly can't make. There are 13, divided into fat-soluble and water-soluble.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c1.text
Human Body: Sailors on long voyages got scurvy: bleeding gums and weakness. In 1747 James Lind showed citrus fruit cured it. Vasco da Gama's crew suffered terribly from it.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c2.text
Human Body: Your skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. It helps absorb calcium for bones. In winter at northern latitudes, many people run low.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c3.text
Human Body: Vitamin A is vital for vision in dim light and for immunity. Carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens provide it as beta-carotene.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c4.text
Human Body: Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods, so people on vegan diets usually need fortified foods or supplements.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c5.text
Human Body: Iron carries oxygen in haemoglobin. Vitamin C helps absorb iron from plants; tea and coffee with meals reduce it.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c6.text
Human Body: About 99% of the body's calcium is in bones and teeth. Dairy, canned fish with bones, tofu and greens are good sources.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c7.text
Human Body: We need some sodium, but most people eat far more than the WHO limit of 5 g of salt a day. Much of it hides in bread, processed meats and ready meals.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c8.text
Human Body: Fibre feeds gut bacteria, keeps digestion regular and helps control blood sugar and cholesterol. Most adults eat too little; aim for about 25–30 g a day.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c9.text
Human Body: For most healthy people, a varied diet supplies what they need. Supplements help in specific cases, like vitamin D in winter or folic acid in pregnancy; more isn't better.

P.title: bo-nutrition.c9.viz.items.0.r
Human Body: Varied food first, supplements for specific needs

P.title: bo-stress.summary
Human Body: Why stress helps, and when it harms.

P.title: bo-stress.q0.q
Human Body: What does the Yerkes–Dodson law say?

P.title: bo-stress.q0.o1
Human Body: Moderate arousal gives the best performance

P.title: bo-stress.q0.x
Human Body: Too little or too much hurts performance.

P.title: bo-stress.q1.q
Human Body: Which system slows the heart and restarts digestion?

P.title: bo-stress.c0.text
Human Body: Stress triggers two systems: a fast nerve response with adrenaline, and a slower hormone response with cortisol, preparing body and mind for a challenge.

P.title: bo-stress.c1.text
Human Body: Short bursts of stress sharpen focus and performance: think of an exam or a race. The problem is stress that never switches off.

P.title: bo-stress.c2.text
Human Body: Performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls. Too little stress is boring; too much overwhelms. Psychologists call it the Yerkes–Dodson law.

P.title: bo-stress.c3.text
Human Body: Long-term stress raises blood pressure and heart-disease risk. Sudden extreme stress can even cause temporary "broken heart syndrome".

P.title: bo-stress.c4.text
Human Body: The gut and brain talk constantly. Stress can cause stomach aches, nausea or bowel changes; "butterflies in the stomach" are real.

P.title: bo-stress.c5.text
Human Body: Brief stress mobilises immune cells; chronic stress suppresses immunity. Students catch more colds during exam season.

P.title: bo-stress.c6.text
Human Body: The parasympathetic system is the counterweight to fight-or-flight: it slows the heart and restarts digestion. Slow breathing switches it on.

P.title: bo-stress.c7.text
Human Body: Evidence-based stress relievers include exercise, sleep, time in nature, talking to friends, slow breathing and limiting news and alcohol.

P.title: bo-stress.c8.text
Human Body: Seeing a pounding heart as "my body getting ready" rather than "I'm panicking" improves performance in studies. How you interpret stress matters.

P.title: bo-stress.c8.viz.items.0.r
Human Body: My body is getting ready to perform

P.title: bo-stress.c9.text
Human Body: Used by pilots and athletes: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times.

P.title: bo-pain.q0.q
Human Body: Why does rubbing a bumped elbow help?

P.title: bo-pain.q0.o1
Human Body: Touch signals compete with pain signals

P.title: bo-pain.q1.q
Human Body: Why can heart problems cause arm pain?

P.title: bo-pain.c0.text
Human Body: Pain warns of damage. People born unable to feel pain often injure themselves badly without noticing.

P.title: bo-pain.c1.text
Human Body: Special nerve endings called nociceptors detect harmful heat, pressure or chemicals and send signals to the spinal cord and brain.

P.title: bo-pain.c2.text
Human Body: Stub a toe and you feel a sharp, quick pain first, then a dull ache. They travel along different nerve fibres at different speeds.

P.title: bo-pain.c3.text
Human Body: Pain is made by the brain, not the injury alone. Attention, fear and context can turn it up or down. Soldiers have ignored serious wounds in battle.

P.title: bo-pain.c4.text
Human Body: Rubbing a bumped elbow helps because touch signals compete with pain signals at "gates" in the spinal cord.

P.title: bo-pain.c5.text
Human Body: Pain can be felt far from its source. Heart problems can show up as arm or jaw pain because nerves share pathways.

P.title: bo-pain.c6.text
Human Body: Many amputees feel the missing limb, sometimes painfully. Mirror therapy, which tricks the brain with a reflection, can help.

P.title: bo-pain.c7.text
Human Body: Paracetamol and anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen work differently. Anti-inflammatories block chemicals that sensitise nerves; opioids act on the brain and spinal cord.

P.title: bo-pain.c8.text
Human Body: A sugar pill can reduce pain when people expect it to, because expectation triggers the brain's own pain-relief chemicals. Placebos work best for pain and nausea.

P.title: bo-pain.c9.text
Human Body: When pain lasts beyond three months, the nervous system itself can become oversensitive. Treatment often combines movement, therapy and medicine.

P.title: bo-odd.q0.x
Human Body: It runs close to the skin.

P.title: bo-odd.q1.q
Human Body: Why are you taller in the morning?

P.title: bo-odd.c0.text
Human Body: Yawning may cool the brain and increase alertness. It's contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can make you yawn.

P.title: bo-odd.c0.viz.items.3
Human Body: Even dogs catch it from us

P.title: bo-odd.c1.text
Human Body: Hiccups are sudden spasms of the diaphragm, with the vocal cords snapping shut to make the "hic". Charles Osborne hiccuped for 68 years.

P.title: bo-odd.c2.text
Human Body: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve some metals, so the stomach renews its protective lining every few days.

P.title: bo-odd.c3.text
Human Body: Fingerprints form before birth and are unique, even between identical twins. They may improve grip and touch sensitivity.

P.title: bo-odd.c4.text
Human Body: Hitting your "funny bone" actually hits the ulnar nerve, which runs close to the skin at the elbow. That's why it tingles down to your little finger.

P.title: bo-odd.c5.text
Human Body: You're about 1 cm taller in the morning: the discs in your spine compress during the day and recover overnight.

P.title: bo-odd.c6.text
Human Body: Borborygmi, stomach rumbles, are gas and fluid moving through the gut. They're loudest when empty because there's less food to muffle them.

P.title: bo-odd.c7.text
Human Body: Cold food on the roof of your mouth makes blood vessels constrict and then quickly widen, causing a sharp headache for a few seconds.

P.title: bo-odd.c8.text
Human Body: Your navel is a scar from the umbilical cord. Belly buttons host hundreds of species of bacteria.

P.title: bo-odd.c9.text
Human Body: About half of people get "frisson", chills from moving music. It's linked to dopamine release at emotional peaks.
